title: Memory Harnesses for Long-Running Research Agents — Stefania Druga, Sakana.ai

primary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
primary.rationale: The entire talk is about memory systems for long-running agents: memory as a write-manage-read control loop, the recall policy ladder (no recall, vector RAG, ranked decisions ledger, oracle), and harness architecture with core/recall/archival blocks. Directly matches inclusion criteria: primary focus is context construction, memory, compaction, or durable conversational state, and engineering the working set the model sees across turns.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: The memory harness wraps around the model as a control-plane component for long-running research agents. The harness architecture (core, recall, archival blocks) and write-manage-read loop are agent-system design concepts, though the primary focus is on the memory and recall policy rather than agent loop or planning design.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: She systematically evaluates recall policies across 68 X-Bench questions and Spider V2 with ablations (arbitrary examples, wrong step, most recent step) and multiple seeds. The experimental methodology is significant but serves the memory research rather than being the primary subject.

secondary.label: Inference & Model Systems
secondary.rationale: Local model deployment on an M3 Ultra with Qwen 27B 4-bit quantization and DeepSeek V4 Flash is discussed as infrastructure, including serial-only execution constraints, but inference performance is not the research focus.

domains.label: Scientific Research
domains.rationale: The talk explicitly focuses on long-running research agents, including a literature review task with a retracted Nature paper and long-horizon research question answering on X-Bench.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The memory harness architecture, recall policy ladder, and findings about when memory adds value versus cost are applicable broadly across agent domains and tasks.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Over 30 runnable memory cookbooks are available in an open-source Diamond repository, providing developer tooling for memory system construction.

summary: Stefania Druga, Staff Research Scientist at Sakana AI's RSI Lab in Tokyo, presents "Memory Harnesses for Long-Running Research Agents" at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. She reframes agent memory as a write-manage-read control loop around the model—not a database store—and designs a harness with three blocks: core (always shown to the agent), recall (where different policies are tested), and archival (cross-session persistence). She tests a recall policy ladder: no recall (baseline), vector RAG, a ranked decisions ledger that tracks and prioritizes per-turn decisions, and an oracle that supplies ground-truth correct memory each loop. On two tasks—a literature review where all papers fit in the context window, and X-Bench where the correct answer at step 124 must be retrieved at step 500—she finds that memory adds only cost when content fits in context (no accuracy gain), but on long-horizon tasks the ranked decisions ledger beats all alternatives across 68 X-Bench questions, including beating a gating approach and even the oracle. The oracle fails to reach ceiling because providing correct memory does not force the model to use it. Bad memory is expensive: it burns tokens and can misdirect the agent; ranked recall is also cheaper. Results generalize across Qwen 27B (4-bit) and DeepSeek V4 Flash on X-Bench and Spider V2. She urges treating recall policy as a first-class metric. Over 30 memory cookbooks exist in a Diamond repository. All experiments ran on a local M3 Ultra (96 GB RAM, 28-core CPU) in Tokyo, driven remotely from her phone, providing full data sovereignty at the cost of serial-only execution for some models.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled system: the AI problem (context rot on long-horizon tasks) motivates the SE solution (memory harness architecture with a write-manage-read control loop), which is evaluated using an SE methodology (recall policy ladder with ablation controls) against AI evaluation paradigms (X-Bench, Spider V2, oracle upper bound). The key insight — that a ranked decisions ledger (SE concept) outperforms even ground-truth oracle memory (AI concept) — bridges both domains: it is simultaneously an engineering recommendation (use ranked recall) and a scientific finding about model behavior (providing correct information does not guarantee its use). The token economics concept ties the AI accuracy findings to SE cost constraints, making the case that recall policy is a first-class metric that lives at the intersection of system design and model capability. Without the SE architecture, the AI findings could not be isolated; without the AI benchmarks, the SE architecture would have no validation. They are co-dependent.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (AIE2026) in San Francisco and the video was published on 2026-08-12. The research was conducted at Sakana AI's RSI Lab, which was announced on 2026-06-05. The speaker was promoted to Staff Research Scientist in June 2026. The talk references an industry projection of longer-horizon tasks converging with fewer model releases 'later this year' (2026), suggesting the research is timely. The ZenML LLMOps Database entry corroborating the findings was published the same day as the video (2026-08-12). Research was verified as of 2026-08-23.
takeaways: Memory is a write-manage-read control loop around the model, not a database you attach to it.
When all relevant content already fits in the context window, a memory harness adds only cost with no accuracy gain, marking a clear boundary of utility.
On long-horizon tasks where the answer sits hundreds of steps outside the context window, the memory harness becomes the entire game.
Across 68 X-Bench questions, a ranked decisions ledger that tracks and prioritizes per-turn decisions outperformed no recall, vector RAG, gating, and even the oracle.
The oracle does not reach ceiling performance because giving a model the correct memory does not force it to use that memory correctly.
Bad memory is expensive: it burns tokens and can send the agent in the wrong direction, so recall policy should be treated as a first-class metric.
The ranked recall approach generalizes across models (Qwen 27B 4-bit, DeepSeek V4 Flash) and benchmarks (X-Bench, Spider V2).
Running locally on an M3 Ultra provides full sovereignty over data and pipeline traces, at the cost of serial-only execution for some models.
The trend toward longer-horizon tasks with fewer model releases makes context-rot management increasingly urgent.
Over 30 runnable memory cookbooks exist in an open-source Diamond repository, spanning simple file-system retrieval to trained memory models.

concepts.name: Context Rot
concepts.explanation: On long-horizon tasks, language models degrade in quality: they contradict themselves, redo completed work, or drift from the original user question. This degradation worsens as task length grows relative to the context window.
concepts.importance: Context rot is the core problem the entire talk addresses. Understanding it is a prerequisite for appreciating why memory harnesses matter and why recall policy must be a first-class metric.

concepts.name: Oracle Ground-Truth Memory
concepts.explanation: An upper-bound recall condition that supplies the correct memory to the model each loop iteration. Despite having perfect information, the oracle does not reach ceiling performance because the model may ignore, misinterpret, or fail to use the provided memory.
concepts.importance: This is a profound finding: the bottleneck is not just retrieval quality but model utilization of retrieved memory. It exposes a gap between information availability and information use that has implications for all RAG and memory systems.

concepts.name: Vector RAG for Agent Memory
concepts.explanation: Standard embedding-based retrieval applied to agent memory: convert past decisions into vectors and retrieve via similarity search. Tested as a rung on the recall policy ladder, it underperforms the ranked decisions ledger on long-horizon tasks.
concepts.importance: Establishes that naive RAG is insufficient for agent memory — the retrieval signal (similarity) does not match what the agent actually needs (decision relevance), motivating the ranked ledger approach.

concepts.name: Long-Horizon Benchmark Design (X-Bench)
concepts.explanation: X-Bench is a benchmark where the correct answer appears at step 124 but the question is asked at step 500, placing the answer 376 steps outside the typical context window. 68 questions are evaluated with multiple seeds.
concepts.importance: X-Bench operationalizes the long-horizon memory problem: it creates a controlled setting where the agent cannot rely on context window alone and must use its memory harness. This benchmark design is itself a contribution.

concepts.name: Token Economics of Memory
concepts.explanation: Memory is not free: bad memory burns tokens by injecting irrelevant information that the model must process, and can misdirect the agent toward wrong actions. Ranked recall reduces cost because it provides relevant, compact memory that the model can act on efficiently.
concepts.importance: Quantifies the cost dimension of memory systems. The finding that ranked recall is cheaper than alternatives (including no recall in some cases) makes the economic case for investing in recall policy engineering.

concepts.name: Context Window Boundary of Utility
concepts.explanation: When all relevant task content fits within the model's context window, a memory harness provides no accuracy improvement and only adds cost (~3x tokens per the speaker's LinkedIn summary). Memory harnesses become valuable only when the answer lies outside the context window.
concepts.importance: Defines the precise boundary condition for when memory systems are worth investing in. This is an actionable engineering decision rule: assess context-fittedness before building a memory pipeline.

concepts.name: Cross-Model and Cross-Benchmark Generalization
concepts.explanation: The ranked recall approach generalizes across two models (Qwen 27B 4-bit and DeepSeek V4 Flash) and two benchmarks (X-Bench and Spider V2), suggesting the finding is not an artifact of a specific model or task.
concepts.importance: Generalization is critical for establishing that ranked recall is a robust engineering principle, not a narrow empirical result. It gives practitioners confidence to apply the approach to their own models and tasks.

concepts.name: Sovereign AI
concepts.explanation: Running models locally provides full sovereignty: complete control over data, pipeline traces, and evaluation provenance. Sakana AI's broader mission includes building frontier AI in Japan with sovereignty as a core principle. The trade-off is serial-only execution and RAM constraints.
concepts.importance: Sovereignty is both a technical and geopolitical framing that motivates local deployment. It contextualizes why the experiments ran on local hardware rather than cloud APIs and connects to Sakana AI's organizational mission.

concepts.name: Memory Harness Architecture
concepts.explanation: A three-block system design for agent memory: a core block always shown to the agent, a recall block where different retrieval policies are tested, and an archival block for cross-session persistence. This architectural pattern separates concerns between what the agent always sees, what is dynamically retrieved, and what survives across runs.
concepts.importance: Provides the structural foundation for the entire talk — all recall policy experiments are conducted within this harness, and the architecture itself is a reusable design pattern for any long-horizon agent system.

concepts.name: Write-Manage-Read Control Loop
concepts.explanation: The conceptual model that memory is not a passive database but an active control loop around the model: write decisions to memory, manage (rank, filter, prioritize) what persists, and read (recall) the right memory at the right time. The manage step is where policy decisions live.
concepts.importance: This reframing is the talk's central thesis. It shifts the engineering mindset from 'attach a vector store' to 'design a control loop,' which changes how memory policies are evaluated and compared.

concepts.name: Ranked Decisions Ledger
concepts.explanation: A data structure and recall policy that tracks per-turn decisions and ranks them by relevance for retrieval. Rather than returning arbitrary or most-recent memory, it prioritizes decisions that are most likely to be needed for the current step.
concepts.importance: This is the winning recall policy across all experiments — it outperformed no recall, vector RAG, gating, and even the oracle on 68 X-Bench questions, making it the key engineering contribution of the talk.

concepts.name: Recall Policy Ladder
concepts.explanation: A systematic evaluation methodology that tests recall policies in order of sophistication: no recall (baseline), vector RAG, ranked decisions ledger, and oracle (ground-truth). The model is held fixed; only the recall policy varies, enabling controlled comparison.
concepts.importance: This ladder is the experimental backbone of the talk. It establishes a reusable evaluation framework for any team comparing memory strategies, and the controlled-variable design is a model for rigorous agent engineering.

concepts.name: Ablation Study Design for Memory
concepts.explanation: The talk includes ablation controls: arbitrary examples, wrong step, and most recent step as recall baselines against the ranked ledger. These controls isolate whether ranked recall wins because of ranking quality or mere recency/arbitrariness.
concepts.importance: The ablation framework provides a ready-made rubric for practitioners to validate their own recall policies and guard against confounds like recency bias.

concepts.name: Local Model Deployment Infrastructure
concepts.explanation: Running all experiments on a local M3 Ultra Mac (96 GB RAM, 28-core CPU) in Tokyo, controlled remotely from a phone, with active cooling during non-stop evaluations. Uses Qwen 27B at 4-bit quantization and DeepSeek V4 Flash.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that frontier agent memory research is feasible on consumer hardware, lowering the barrier to entry. The deployment setup is a reproducible engineering reference for practitioners without cloud GPU budgets.

concepts.name: Serial Execution Constraint
concepts.explanation: Local models like DeepSeek V4 Flash run serially only and do not support batch querying, making large-scale evaluation slow. This is a fundamental trade-off of local sovereignty: full control over data and pipeline at the cost of throughput.
concepts.importance: Highlights a critical engineering constraint for local agent deployment: evaluation throughput is bottlenecked by serial execution, which affects experimental design, iteration speed, and scale of ablation studies.

concepts.name: Gating Mechanism for Memory Invocation
concepts.explanation: A policy that asks whether memory is needed at each step before invoking recall. The talk tests this as an alternative to always-on ranked recall and finds it underperforms the ranked ledger.
concepts.importance: Gating is a natural engineering optimization (skip memory when not needed to save cost), but the finding that it underperforms ranked recall challenges the assumption that selective memory invocation is always better.

sections.title: Context rot and the long-horizon trend
sections.summary: Stefania introduces the problem of context blow on long-horizon tasks: models contradict themselves, redo work, or drift from questions. Industry projections show longer-horizon tasks converging with fewer model releases, making context rot a priority.

sections.title: Local models and the Tokyo machine
sections.summary: Local models like GLM and DeepSeek V4 Flash are crossing the usefulness line for agentic tasks. Coinbase reduced AI spend by moving to local models with better routing and caching. Her setup: M3 Ultra with 96 GB RAM, 28-core CPU in Tokyo, controlled from her phone, running Qwen 27B 4-bit and DeepSeek V4 Flash, with fans cooling it during non-stop evals.

sections.title: Memory as a write-manage-read control loop
sections.summary: Memory should be understood as a write-manage-read control loop around the model, not a database store. The harness design has a core block always shown to the agent, a recall block for testing different modes, and an archival block for cross-session information.

sections.title: The recall ladder
sections.summary: The recall block tests a ladder: no recall (baseline), vector RAG, a ranked decisions ledger that tracks and prioritizes per-turn decisions, and an oracle that supplies ground-truth correct memory each loop. The model is held fixed; only the recall policy varies.

sections.title: Task one: literature review with a retracted claim
sections.summary: A literature review corpus includes a retracted Nature paper claiming 742,000 promising materials. Because all papers fit in the context window, memory added no capability improvement, only cost. When the task fits in context, the harness does not help.

sections.title: Task two: X-Bench long-horizon retrieval
sections.summary: X-Bench tests long-horizon memory: the correct answer is at step 124 but the question is asked at step 500, far outside the context window. The model must use the memory harness to retrieve the answer from the right step.

sections.title: Results: ranked ledger wins across 68 questions
sections.summary: Across 68 X-Bench questions with multiple seeds, the rank-only decisions ledger performed best, beating even a gating approach. The oracle does not hit max because providing correct memory does not force the model to use it. Ablations with arbitrary examples, wrong steps, and recent steps all confirm ranked recall wins.

sections.title: Generalization and cost
sections.summary: The ranked recall approach works across models (Qwen 27B, DS4 Flash) and benchmarks (X-Bench, Spider V2). It costs less than alternatives, supporting the heuristic that bad memory is expensive because it burns tokens and misdirects the agent.

sections.title: Recall policy as a first-class metric
sections.summary: She urges the audience to treat recall policy as a first-class metric: what memories to store, how to rank them, how to design the recall function, and what survives across sessions and runs.

sections.title: Wider landscape, local sovereignty, and Sakana
sections.summary: The memory technique landscape is rich, with over 30 runnable cookbooks in a Diamond repository spanning simple retrieval to trained memory models. Running locally gave her full control over data and pipeline traces, an example of sovereignty, at the cost of serial-only execution. This connects to Sakana AI's sovereign AI mission in Japan; they are hiring.

organization.name: Sakana AI
organization.summary: Sakana AI is a Tokyo-based frontier AI R&D company founded in July 2023 by David Ha (CEO), Ren Ito (Chairman), and Llion Jones (CTO). The company focuses on nature-inspired intelligence, recursive self-improvement (RSI), and autonomous research agents. Their RSI Lab, where the speaker works, is a dedicated research group tasked with redesigning the AI development process itself with AI. Sakana AI is known for technologies including The AI Scientist (published in Nature, March 2026), the Darwin Godel Machine, ShinkaEvolve, and Multi-Agent Orchestration Foundation Models. The company has raised approximately $200M in Series A funding from investors including NEA, Khosla Ventures, Lux Capital, and NVIDIA, and employs approximately 164 people across 10 countries.

technologies.label: Memory Harness with Write-Manage-Read Control Loop
technologies.primary: Memory Harness with Write-Manage-Read Control Loop
technologies.summary: The memory harness is the central architecture of the talk. It reframes agent memory from a passive database store to an active write-manage-read control loop wrapped around the model: write decisions to memory, manage (rank, filter, prioritize) what persists, and read (recall) the right memory at the right time. The harness has three blocks: a core block always shown to the agent, a recall block where different retrieval policies are tested, and an archival block for cross-session persistence. A critical finding is the boundary of utility: when all task content fits within the context window, the harness adds only cost (~3x tokens) with no accuracy improvement, but on long-horizon tasks where answers lie far outside the context window, the harness becomes essential.
technologies.role: Central architecture — the entire talk is structured around this harness design, its evaluation across recall policies, and the finding that memory management is a control loop rather than a data store.

technologies.label: Ranked Decisions Ledger
technologies.summary: A recall policy that tracks per-turn decisions and ranks them by relevance for retrieval. Rather than returning arbitrary, most-recent, or similarity-based memory, it prioritizes decisions most likely needed for the current step. Across 68 X-Bench questions with multiple seeds, the ranked decisions ledger outperformed no recall, vector RAG, gating, and even the oracle. The finding that it beats the oracle is profound: providing correct memory does not guarantee the model uses it, so a structured ranking that guides the model toward relevant decisions is more effective than perfect information. The ranked ledger also costs fewer tokens than alternatives, supporting the heuristic that bad memory is expensive. Results generalize across two models (Qwen 27B 4-bit, DeepSeek V4 Flash) and two benchmarks (X-Bench, Spider V2).
technologies.role: The key experimental result and primary engineering contribution — the winning recall policy that outperforms all alternatives including the oracle upper bound.

technologies.label: Local Model Inference on Apple Silicon
technologies.primary: Local Model Inference on Apple M3 Ultra
technologies.summary: All experiments were conducted on a local Apple Mac Studio with M3 Ultra chip (96 GB unified memory, 28-core CPU) in Tokyo, driven remotely from the speaker's phone with active cooling during non-stop evaluations. Two models were used: Qwen 27B at 4-bit quantization and DeepSeek V4 Flash. This setup provided full data sovereignty — complete control over data, pipeline traces, and evaluation provenance — at the cost of serial-only execution for DeepSeek V4 Flash, which does not support batch querying. The speaker connected this to Sakana AI's broader sovereign AI mission in Japan and noted that local models are crossing the usefulness line for agentic tasks, citing Coinbase's reported cost savings from shifting to local models with better routing and caching.
technologies.role: The local inference infrastructure that enabled all memory harness experiments, providing full data sovereignty at the cost of serial execution throughput.

technologies.label: Long-Horizon Agent Memory Benchmarks
technologies.summary: X-Bench is the primary evaluation benchmark designed for long-horizon memory: the correct answer appears at step 124 but the question is asked at step 500, placing the answer 376 steps outside the context window. 68 questions are evaluated with multiple seeds and cells. Spider V2 (Spider 2.0) was used as a second benchmark to validate that ranked recall generalizes beyond a single evaluation setting. The benchmark design itself is a contribution — it creates a controlled setting where the agent cannot rely on the context window alone and must use its memory harness, enabling rigorous comparison of recall policies.
technologies.role: Evaluation infrastructure that operationalizes the long-horizon memory problem and enables rigorous comparison of recall policies.

Understanding of RAG and memory retrieval concepts including vector search and embedding-based retrieval

Exposure to agent architecture patterns including tool use, multi-step reasoning, and state management
Foundational understanding of experimental design including baselines, ablations, and controlled comparisons
outcomes: Identify when a memory harness adds value (long-horizon, out-of-context tasks) versus when it only adds cost (everything fits in context), and articulate the boundary of utility

Design a memory harness as a write-manage-read control loop with three components: a core block always shown to the agent, a recall block for testing different policies, and an archival block for cross-session persistence
Evaluate recall policies using a ladder from baseline (no recall) through vector RAG, ranked decisions ledger, and oracle ground-truth, and explain why each rung matters
Treat recall policy as a first-class metric alongside accuracy and cost, understanding that bad memory is expensive because it burns tokens and can misdirect the agent
Explain why providing correct memory via an oracle is insufficient without mechanisms to ensure the model actually uses that memory, and design interventions to address this gap
Conduct ablation studies on memory policies using arbitrary examples, wrong steps, and most recent steps as controls against ranked recall
Assess the trade-offs of local model deployment for sovereign AI: full control over data and pipeline traces versus serial-only execution constraints and RAM bottlenecks
challengeSeeds: Build a memory harness with core, recall, and archival blocks; implement no-recall, vector-RAG, and ranked-ledger policies; evaluate on a synthetic 500-step task where the answer is at step 124
Design an intervention that closes the gap between oracle and ranked-ledger performance by improving how the model uses retrieved memory, not just what is retrieved
Construct a cost-accuracy trade-off curve across recall policies and identify the Pareto-optimal operating point for a given token budget
Run ablations with arbitrary examples, wrong steps, and most recent steps as recall controls; compare degradation patterns to the ranked ledger
Port the ranked decisions ledger to a different model family (e.g., a Llama variant) and test generalization on a second long-horizon benchmark
Implement a gating mechanism that decides whether to invoke memory at all, and measure at what context-fittedness threshold gating saves cost without sacrificing accuracy
